item.title: Sparse-to-Sparse Feature Learning for Cross-Layer Analysis and Steering
item.description:
Authors: Masahiro Kaneko, Ayana Niwa, Timothy Baldwin

Understanding how models internally represent information is a central challenge in interpretation and control. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose dense hidden representations into sparse features, and cross-layer methods capture structure spanning multiple layers. However, existing objectives do not explicitly train the sparse code at one layer to predict the sparse code at the next layer. item.title: Social Bias Neurons in Multilingual Language Models: A Mechanistic Interpretability Analysis
item.description:
Authors: Lance Calvin Lim Gamboa, Yue Feng, Mark Lee

Multilingual models exhibit social bias when processing inputs pertaining to societal stereotypes. We adapt emerging mechanistic interpretability methods to pinpoint and characterize model components that encode this bias. We conduct our analysis across three instruction-tuned models, four languages, and seven bias dimensions. item.description:
Authors: Yuchen Zhu, Sergio Hernan Garrido Mejia, Dominik Janzing

Existing frameworks in causal abstraction first propose a high-level causal model, and then verify whether its interventional effects agree with those of a given micro-level model - the two models are declared causally consistent when the discrepancy is zero. item.description:
Authors: Mingyu Kim, Doguk Kim

Time series transformers have achieved strong forecasting performance, yet it remains unclear which of their components, attention or the feed-forward network (FFN), constructs temporal features, and how tokenization such as patching changes this. item.title: MonoQPM: Splitting Features into Concepts for Inherent Interpretability and Predictive Performance
item.description:
Authors: Thomas Norrenbrock, Robert Zimmermann, Timo Kaiser, Sovan Biswas, Neslihan Kose, et al.

Alongside superposition, polysemanticity is one of the primary obstacles to achieving interpretable deep neural networks. While these phenomena are typically intrinsically linked, the Quadratic Programming Enhanced Model (QPM) naturally decouples them. By representing classes with a sparse binary assignment of very few features, QPM prevents superposition by design on its final features but still exhibits polysemanticity. However, measuring polysemanticity is an open problem. This work proposes

item.title: Beyond Patching: Consistent Circuit Discovery via Gradient Spectral Analysis
item.description:
Authors: Yujie Zhang, Tianyi Zhao, Guanghui Min, Chen Chen

Mechanistic interpretability seeks to reverse-engineer neural networks by identifying small, faithful subgraphs--circuits--that implement specific behaviors. The dominant paradigm scores each unit by replacing its clean activation with a corrupted counterpart as causal intervention. While effective, this approach rests on a brittle prerequisite: the structure prompt pairs are task-specific, expensive to engineer, and silently couple the discovered circuit to prompt-design choices. item.title: What Remains After Concept Erasure? Sparse Autoencoder Probes for Auditing Diffusion Models
item.description:
Authors: Zhuan Shi, Lu Wei, Yuta Nakashima, Noa Garcia, Golnoosh Farnadi

Concept erasure aims to remove selected visual concepts from text-to-image diffusion models while preserving the generation of non-target concepts. Evaluation typically measures target suppression and non-target preservation in generated images, but a concept's absence from these outputs does not establish its removal from the model. item.title: Uncovering Separable and Composable Skill Mechanisms in Vision-Language Models
item.description:
Authors: Miaoyu Li, Boyang Li

Recent work has sought to localize the internal mechanisms underlying visual reasoning skills in vision-language models. These methods largely overlook separability and composability in both mechanism identification and evaluation. We propose separability and composability as two important desiderata for skill localization. Separability requires identified mechanisms to contribute primarily to their target skills while having limited effects on other skills, enabling precise diagnosis and target

Tags: vision, reasoning

item.title: SAE-Audit: Clinical-Trial Prediction via Inference-Time Optimization of Black-Box LLMs Audited by Sparse Autoencoder Evidence
item.description:
Authors: Junbo Shen

Clinical trials are costly and often take years to complete, making early outcome prediction valuable for trial planning. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to forecast clinical-trial outcomes, yet their predictions remain unreliable and their rationales may not faithfully reflect the evidence underlying their answers. On tasks such as predicting whether a registered clinical trial will complete or terminate early, frontier LLMs perform only modestly above chance in our experimen

item.title: Compared to What? Calibrating Machine-Unlearning Diagnostics with Present, Absent and Suppressed Anchors
item.description:
Authors: Arsalan Kaleem

Unlearning methods for language models are judged mainly by behaviour, but a model can stop producing an answer while still encoding it. Internal diagnostics such as linear probes, the logit lens and relearning speed are used to tell removal from suppression, yet none has been checked against cases where the answer is known. item.title: PatchLens: Adapting Mechanistic Interpretability Techniques for Non-Expert Audiences
item.description:
Authors: Gwenyth Lincroft, Yik Su Chan, Adam Belfki, Emma Bortz, Jonathan Bell

A chat interface presents a reply as finished text, concealing a model that predicts at every position and reruns. Mechanistic interpretability can show how a large language model produces text, but its tools are built for researchers. We present PatchLens, a browser interface that runs logit lens and activation patching on remotely served research-scale models. item.title: WaXup: Weight Averaging of Experts as Data Augmentation for Robust Introspection
item.description:
Authors: Marc Boëlle, Lucas Dixon, Alexandre Ramé

As the capabilities of large language models keep improving, traditional mechanistic interpretability methods struggle to keep pace. In contrast, trainable introspection methods emerge as a promising alternative; they repurpose the model itself as a self-diagnostic tool, trained to verbalize what it has learned during finetuning in natural language. item.title: Weight-space programming and mechanistic interpretability for model editing in particle physics
item.description:
Authors: Raphaël Bonnet-Guerrini, Johann Ioannou-Nikolaides, Troels Petersen

We demonstrate that weight-space programming and edits guided by sparse autoencoders can remove unwanted aspects of a particle-physics foundation model through direct edits to its weights. item.title: Auditing Post-Training Unlearning in Diffusion Language Models using Sparse Autoencoders
item.description:
Authors: Yunha Seo, Changhoon Kim

Machine unlearning is an approach to privacy protection: it aims to remove the influence of designated data while preserving the model's behavior on information that should be retained. While a growing body of work investigates this objective in autoregressive large language models, machine unlearning remains underexplored in diffusion language models (DLMs). item.description:
Authors: James Baker

Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose diffusion model activations into interpretable features, but steering a model with them requires identifying which features map to a given semantic concept, if any. Existing methods for this concept to feature task are expensive, relying on grid searches or repeated passes through the frozen UNet. We propose Efficient Semantic Sparse Identification (ESSI). item.title: Who Moved My $Z$ Boson? Revealing Resonance Features Inside a Neural Network
item.description:
Authors: Kevin Alberto Urquía Calderón, Midori Kato, Inar Timiryasov, Oleg Ruchayskiy

Methods used in mechanistic interpretability have revealed human-aligned concepts inside language and image models. In this paper, we search for physics concepts inside a neural a generative collider physics model trained on real LHC data (ShellFlow). We discover features inside ShellFlow that represent resonances, such as the $Z$, $J/ψ$, and $Υ$. item.title: Revealing Pathway Interactions in Network Computations with Complete Path Contribution
item.description:
Authors: Shenghua Liu, Youssef Faragalla, Surya Ganguli, Stephen A. Baccus

Networks pass signals through many layers of interconnected units, so explaining what they compute means tracing how information travels from input to output and how pathways interact. Most existing approaches analyze only pairwise interactions between components such as units, layers or attention heads. item.title: Parasite Features: Causal Abstraction Through Spurious Pathways
item.description:
Authors: Denis Sutter, Qing Yao, Sasha Boguraev, Julian Minder, Antonio Di Maio, et al.

Causal Abstraction defines a notion of \emph{equivalence} between a neural network and an algorithm, thus serving as a powerful framework for mechanistic interpretability. In this paper, however, we show the existence of a class of \emph{spurious features} which straightforwardly pass such equivalence tests. Suppose there are two directions in a model's representation space where: (i) one discriminates the input based on some feature, and (ii) the other steers the model towards a certain output.

item.title: From Observation to Explanation: Mechanistic Interpretability of LLM-Generated Code for Principled Repair
item.description:
Authors: Musfiqur Rahman

Large language models (LLMs) have transformed software development, yet our understanding of how they generate code remains critically underdeveloped. We address this gap by triangulating evidence across three layers. Longitudinally, autonomous agent-attributed code is statistically indistinguishable from human code under a semantic modification definition (HR = 1.019, p = 0.490), yet attracts disproportionately corrective modifications in production (49.1% vs 37.9% human baseline). item.title: Harmonic Circuit: Chord Progression Lies in a Sparse Principal Information Flow in Symbolic Music Models
item.description:
Authors: Ruiji Yu, Gus Xia

Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) seeks to decode neural network computations into human-understandable logic. A core methodology in MI is circuit discovery: identifying the information flow in sub-networks that drive specific model behaviors. While circuit discovery has matured within Natural Language Processing (NLP), the interpretable circuits in music models remain largely unexplored. item.title: GateWatch: Low-Overhead LLM Monitoring with Boolean Circuits
item.description:
Authors: Firas Spanioli, Yaniv David

As large language models (LLMs) and LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed, monitoring their behavior becomes important for detecting unsafe or unintended actions. Activation probes offer an efficient approach, but existing methods face trade-offs between accuracy, interpretability, and computational overhead. item.title: Separating Interpretability and Reconstruction in Sparse Autoencoders
item.description:
Authors: Anh Tien Nguyen, Dimitris Samaras, Mahdi S. Hosseini

Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are effective tools for mechanistic interpretability by decomposing neural representations into sparse and interpretable features. However, a single sparse representation in traditional SAEs is responsible for both reconstruction fidelity and interpretability, which are not guaranteed to align. item.title: Auditing Learned Dynamics in Weather Models
item.description:
Authors: Skylar Gu, Christina Last

Learned weather models are experimentally accessible computational systems whose internal representations can be inspected and manipulated. Using sparse autoencoder features from GraphCast, DeepMind's autoregressive weather forecasting model, we test whether causal relevance requires physical semantics, a question that matters for auditing whether AI forecasters used in high-assurance settings rely on reliable mechanisms. item.title: Tracking Representations in LLM Reasoning Traces for Iterated Games
item.description:
Authors: Chaipat Tirapongprasert, Rajarshi Das, Parijat Dube

Large language model (LLM) agents achieve state-of-the-art performance across domains through chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning. Despite their ubiquitous use, little is understood about the relationship between the externalized trace and the model's actual computation. We address this by investigating how LLM agents make decisions in iterative games with incomplete information. item.title: Abstention Direction in Large Language Models: Mechanistic Interpretability of Abstention Across Query Ambiguity, Knowledge Limits, and Safety Alignment
item.description:
Authors: Koki Itai, Jun Hirako, Hiroaki Yamagiwa

Abstention, the withholding of a response by a large language model (LLM) under uncertainty or safety risks, is essential for trustworthy models. The causes of abstention fall into three perspectives: ambiguity in the Query (Q), limits of Model Knowledge (MK), and misalignment with Human Values (HV). However, prior analyses of internal representations have focused on HV, using a refusal direction computed from harmful and harmless queries. No study has analyzed the three perspectives jointly. We

item.title: Pretty Linear Liars: Unregularized Probes Favor Intervention-Unfaithful Features
item.description:
Authors: Karl Vilhelmsson Emneby, Julian Yocum, Cameron Allen

Linear probing is a common technique in mechanistic interpretability despite the fact that the decodability of a given feature does not necessarily imply the network uses that feature. Intervention faithfulness, not merely decodability, is the appropriate criterion for whether a feature serves a defined active role in the model. item.description:
Authors: Yisong Cao, Leah Kim, Brian Wright, Ali Rivera

Job titles and job descriptions alone provide limited insight into how technical roles differ in a changing job market. To assess how such roles differ in their work and industry applications, we design and compare two methods based on deep learning and transformer representations using 36,081 early-career job postings collected from LinkedIn in the United States between December 2025 and October 2026. item.title: Representational Change Under Self-Consuming Training: A Sparse Autoencoder Analysis
item.description:
Authors: Suchit Gupte, Zhongteng Cai, Xueru Zhang, Mohammad Mahdi Khalili

Large language models are increasingly exposed to model-generated text, raising the possibility that future models will be trained recursively on the outputs of their predecessors. Prior work on such self-consuming training loops has largely focused on output quality and downstream performance, leaving their effects on internal representations poorly understood. item.description:
Authors: Lion Jasper Gleiter, Tingying Peng

Image-based classification of organoid morphologies can indicate drug response, viability, or successful differentiation. In recent work, learned representations outperform handcrafted features as the basis for downstream classifiers. However, their black-box nature hides the morphological cues a classifier relies on. item.description:
Authors: Davide Liga, Liuwen Yu, Matteo Magnini

Interpretability methods can locate the attention heads and sparse autoencoder (SAE) features that change the answer a language model gives to a moral prompt, e.g., whether "Stealing medicine for a dying child is morally" continues with "justified" or "wrong".
